questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain how coordinate rates determine speed
questions.stem: In the log, how is the speed of a bee computed from the rates at which its coordinates change?

answer.exemplar: The velocity of the bee is the pair of rates, dx/dt and dy/dt, and the speed is the magnitude of that vector, the square root of the sum of the squares of the two rates. The speed is therefore always a nonnegative number: it records how fast the distance from the start is growing rather than which way the bee is heading, and it is the quantity one integrates to obtain the total distance travelled over an interval of time.

questions.explanation: The velocity is the pair of coordinate rates, and the speed is its magnitude, the square root of the sum of the squared rates. Speed discards direction, so it is nonnegative and measures how fast the distance from the start grows.
questions.hint: Speed is the magnitude of the pair of coordinate rates.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the formula for the distance from the origin to a line
questions.stem: In the log, why is the distance from the origin to a line written as a constant divided by the length of the normal?

answer.exemplar: The line Ax + By = C has a normal vector (A, B), and the distance along that normal from the origin to the line is the distance travelled before the left-hand side reaches the value C. questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain why polar to Cartesian conversion needs a sine and a cosine
questions.stem: In the log, why does converting a polar entry to Cartesian coordinates need both a cosine and a sine?

answer.exemplar: The polar entry fixes a direction, given by the angle, and a distance, given by the radius. The cosine of the angle gives the horizontal share of that direction and the sine gives the vertical share, and multiplying each share by the radius gives the two coordinates of the point. Using only one of them would record only a single projection, while the pair together places the point unambiguously on the plane.

questions.explanation: The angle gives a direction, and the cosine and sine of that angle give its horizontal and vertical shares. Multiplying each share by the radius produces the two coordinates that pin the point down on the plane.
questions.hint: The angle gives a direction, the radius gives a distance.

questions.stem: How does the polar area formula build up the area of a region, and where does the one half come from?

answer.exemplar: The region is cut into thin wedges, each spanning a small angle dtheta, and each wedge is treated as a triangle with two sides of length r meeting at the origin, so its area is one half of r squared dtheta. questions.topic: Distance from the origin to a line
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the normal length in the line distance
questions.stem: In the log, why does the distance from the origin to a line depend on the size of the normal vector?

answer.exemplar: The normal vector (A, B) measures the rate at which the line equation changes as a point moves perpendicular to the line, so a short normal means the constant C is reached after a long walk, and a long normal means it is reached sooner.
